answer: For agents diagnosing ivory-colored lesions on willow leaves, the allocation kernel can demand concurrent memory proofs. Each claimant commits to a distinct, slowly encoded 1 GB buffer before unpredictable probes request random blocks under a tight deadline. Reusing one buffer across keys fails verification. An attacker running 1,000 aliases must keep about 1 TB resident or pay to recompute within the deadline. This raises hardware and power costs; security depends on sound encoding and calibrated timing.
